suite_baseline.reconciliation: As recorded in parity/control-plane.ledger.json: 2194 collected + 5 modules skipped at collection time = 2199. Unchanged by this belt.

subsystem.name: secretary
subsystem.note: Gate item 8's rehearsal, interlock tests/secretary, 2 files. One ledger per source file (D-0019). The belt is the behavioural and structural halves of a REHEARSAL (interlock Issue #21, interlock D-0022), not item 8's discharge; interlock Q-0011 is open and no numeric latency threshold is stated or used anywhere in the belt.

file.note: The inventory is `pytest --collect-only -q` on the source at 65f36c5, in collection order; all 6 pass there (measured 2026-08-29 against the shared read-only clone of interlock at 65f36c5, `PYTHONPATH=src PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 -m pytest -q tests/secretary/ -p no:cacheprovider`: 11 passed, of which 6 are tests/secretary/test_behaviour.py's).

systematic_mappings.from: `threading.Thread(target=consumer, daemon=True)` + `t.start()` -- a real OS thread running the consumer
systematic_mappings.to: an immediately-invoked `async` arrow function, held as a promise and awaited in an `onTestFinished` teardown
systematic_mappings.why: The source needs a thread because CPython can only make progress on the consumer while the producer is between bytecodes. Node's consumer and producer share one isolate, so the consumer is an asynchronous participant on the same loop. What the source's thread is FOR -- a consumer that has started, has not finished, and is not being driven by the code doing the submitting -- is exactly what the async function gives, and the assertions read the same facts. Recorded as `adapted` on all three stall cases rather than `ported`, because the mechanism changed even though no assertion did.

systematic_mappings.to: the local `stall()` helper: `promise` is what a consumer parks on, `release()` is `set()`, `released` is `is_set()`
systematic_mappings.why: One helper, because the three cases stall the same way; but each case keeps its own distinct observable of WHAT has started -- case 1 reads the queue depth the source asserts, case 2 publishes a named `stage` (`in-work`, reached only after `takeBatch` returned), case 3 reads a shared flag written by a parked OS thread. Sharing the helper without sharing the observable is what stops two cases from going green on each other's evidence.

systematic_mappings.from: `assert judgement_started.wait(timeout=30), "consumer never picked up"` -- a bounded wait whose timeout is documented as test mechanics, not an acceptance number
systematic_mappings.to: `await judgementStarted.promise` followed by an assertion on the flag, with the runner's own `testTimeout` (60s, vitest.config.ts) as the only bound
systematic_mappings.why: The source says in its module docstring that the `join`/`wait` timeouts only bound how long a FAILING run hangs. Continuo already has exactly that bound configured once, for every test, with a written rationale -- so the port takes it from there rather than restating a number per case. The assertion that follows the await is not redundant: it is the source's `"consumer never picked up"` message, kept, and it is what distinguishes a released stall from a resolved one if the helper is ever changed.

systematic_mappings.from: `while not queue.take_batch(limit=N): pass` -- a busy spin in the consumer thread
systematic_mappings.why: A bare spin cannot work on one loop: the consumer would never yield and the producer would never run. `setImmediate` rather than `Promise.resolve()` because a microtask-only yield hands control back to the same continuation queue and can starve the rest of the loop. This is test mechanics -- how one asynchronous participant lets another run -- and never a wait for a duration.

systematic_mappings.from: `os.pipe()` + a monitor thread parked in `os.read(r_fd, 1)`, released by `os.write(w_fd, b"x")`, with `t.is_alive()` as the proof it was still parked
systematic_mappings.to: a `worker_threads` worker (loaded with `eval: true`) parked in `Atomics.wait` on a `SharedArrayBuffer` flag, released by `Atomics.store` + `Atomics.notify`, with `Atomics.load(flag, 0) === 0` and an unreceived `released` message as the proof it was still parked
systematic_mappings.why: This is the one case whose SUBJECT is a genuinely blocked thread -- the C2 analogue of U6 -- so the port keeps a real OS thread really stopped by the kernel rather than an event-loop stand-in. `Atomics.wait` states the same fact as the blocking read (`this thread is stopped until I say otherwise`) without a file descriptor pair to close in teardown, and the proof is stronger than `is_alive()`: the flag is a value THIS test is the only writer of, so `0` means the release has not happened, where a live thread could in principle be live for another reason.

systematic_mappings.to: `onTestFinished` registered at the point the consumer (or worker) is created
systematic_mappings.why: Convention rule 1: cleanup at the acquisition site. It also survives a failure part-way through setup, which a `finally` opened after the `start()` does not -- and it releases the stall even when an assertion above it threw, which is what stops one red case from hanging the file.

Same clock class (monotonic, nanosecond) and same width. `bigint` rather than `number` because a JavaScript double cannot carry a nanosecond stamp exactly and Python's `int` can; the comparison is the source's, an ORDER check and never a threshold (interlock Q-0011 is open).

A Python list is an ordered sequence, as is a JS array, and the source compares positionally. `ACCEPTED` and `REFUSED_QUEUE_FULL` are imported from `src/secretary/intake.js` rather than spelled as literals, exactly as the source imports them from `claude_org_runtime.secretary.intake` rather than from the package barrel -- the vocabulary is deliberately not on the barrel (D-0701).

target_only_tests.why: None. Every collected test in this file is a translation of a source case. The concurrent-producer case's interleaving witness is an assertion INSIDE the adapted case rather than a separate target-only test, because it is what makes that case's own subject (concurrency) real in this runtime -- see its entry.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: No case asserts anything about latency -- not a bound, not a ratio, not a comparison of the stalled run against a baseline.
inherited_limitations.why: interlock Q-0011 is unresolved and the source deliberately invents no threshold. The empirical half of item 8 lives outside this suite (the source points at `investigation/i16_item8_rehearsal.py`), and this belt does not port an investigation script. Adding any number here would turn a rehearsal into a criterion the project has not agreed (D-0701).

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The three stall cases prove the intake answers while ONE consumer is stalled at one site. Nothing asserts the intake answers while all three are stalled at once, or under a realistic number of consumers.
inherited_limitations.why: The source's own scope. Item 8's discharge is the real Secretary under genuine worker load, before the canary starts (interlock D-0022); this is its rehearsal. Widening the cases here would assert more than the source (`docs/test-translation-conventions.md` rule 0) and would still not be the discharge.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `SecretaryIntake` and `IntakeQueue` hold their state in memory, so no case says anything about what a restart does to an accepted-but-undrained request.
inherited_limitations.why: Spike scaffold, throwaway by default (interlock D-0026). Durable intake is the real Secretary's concern and is explicitly not rehearsed.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: Case 3 proves the intake answers while a worker thread is parked; it does not prove that a Secretary built on this intake would keep answering if the MAIN thread were the one doing the blocking read.
inherited_limitations.why: The source has the same limitation and states it: the hazard it models lives in supervisor code, and the property under test is that no lock, queue or call edge connects that code to the intake. A single-isolate runtime makes the counterfactual worse, not different -- which is exactly why the structural half bans synchronous I/O from the package at all.

entries.target_id: test/secretary/behaviour.test.ts::the intake answers while every consumer stalls > intake answers while an AI judgement is in flight
entries.reason: Every assertion the source makes survives, in the source's order: 32 receipts all ACCEPTED, every `answeredNs >= receivedNs`, `queue.depth() === 32` (the consumer made no progress), and the stall demonstrably still unreleased. What changed is the mechanism the stall is built from -- an OS thread parked on a `threading.Event` becomes an async consumer parked on a Promise this file holds the only resolver for -- so the case is `adapted` rather than `ported` even though nothing it asserts moved. The 'proved nothing' guard is kept and strengthened from `not judgement_done.is_set() and t.is_alive()` to `judgementDone.released || consumerCompleted` being false, which reads the same two facts without asking the runtime whether a thread happens to be alive. Measured: releasing the stall before the submits turns the case red.

entries.target_id: test/secretary/behaviour.test.ts::the intake answers while every consumer stalls > intake answers while long-running work holds the consumer
entries.reason: Same adaptation as the case above, same boundary, different stall site: the consumer took its batch of 8 and is stuck in the WORK, after `takeBatch` returned. Both of the source's assertions survive -- 32 receipts all ACCEPTED, and the stall still in force (`not work_done.is_set() and t.is_alive()`). The source asserts no queue depth here and neither does the port, which is deliberate: adding one would assert more than the source (rule 0). The case's distinct observable is instead a named `stage` reaching `in-work`, which is only reachable after `takeBatch` returned -- the fact the source's `work_started.wait()` was establishing.

entries.target_id: test/secretary/behaviour.test.ts::the intake answers while every consumer stalls > intake answers while worker monitoring blocks its thread
entries.reason: The pipe is replaced by a `worker_threads` worker parked in `Atomics.wait` on a shared flag; both are a real OS thread stopped by the kernel and released by the test in teardown, which is the property the source's docstring names ('the stalled thread is parked on an Event or a pipe that this test controls and has not released'). Both of the source's assertions survive: the monitor was still parked when the receipts were taken, and all 32 are ACCEPTED. The 'unblocked early' proof is stronger than `t.is_alive()` -- the flag is a value this test is the only writer of, so reading 0 means the release has not happened. Measured: releasing the worker before the submits turns the case red.

entries.target_id: test/secretary/behaviour.test.ts::the intake answers while every consumer stalls > a full queue is an immediate recorded refusal
entries.reason: Straight transcription. Capacity 2, three submits, two accepted and the third REFUSED_QUEUE_FULL with `answeredNs >= receivedNs`; the refusal log holds exactly that one request id at depth 2; and the drain returns exactly the first two ids in order, so the refusal consumed no capacity and lost no accepted item. Only runtime spellings changed (a generator expression over `range(3)` becomes `[0, 1, 2].map(...)`, Python list equality becomes `toEqual`).

entries.target_id: test/secretary/behaviour.test.ts::the intake answers while every consumer stalls > the boundary is FIFO and pull-only
entries.reason: Straight transcription. An empty queue yields `[]` at once, the first `takeBatch(3)` returns the first three request ids in submission order, the depth is then 2, and the second batch returns the remaining two in order. Only runtime spellings changed (list slicing and comprehensions become `slice` and `map`; `== []` becomes `toEqual([])`).

entries.target_id: test/secretary/behaviour.test.ts::the intake answers while every consumer stalls > concurrent producers never lose or duplicate a request
entries.reason: Re-defined by D-0701 and the one deliberate divergence in the belt. Eight threads become eight producers interleaved on the event loop, each yielding between submits. Every assertion about identity and conservation survives unchanged: 400 receipts, 400 distinct request ids, accepted + refused == 400, the drain holds exactly as many items as were accepted with distinct ids, and the refusal log holds exactly as many entries as there were refusals. The ONE assertion that changed is the capacity bound: the source writes `100 <= len(accepted) <= 100 + 8 - 1`, tolerating the `P - 1` overshoot its lock-free check-then-append race can produce under the GIL. That race cannot occur here -- `submit()` is synchronous and run-to-completion -- so the tolerance is not carried and the accepted count is asserted EXACTLY 100. Carrying it would have been the weaker case: an implementation that had started dropping or duplicating requests could still land inside the window. Because 'concurrent' now means interleaving rather than parallelism, the case also witnesses the interleaving (no producer's request ids are contiguous), so a serial run cannot satisfy it; measured -- removing the yield between submits turns the case red.
